content: Saussurea is a genus comprising approximately 300 species of flowering plants within the family Asteraceae. These plants are native to cool temperate and arctic regions across Asia, Europe, and North America, with the greatest diversity found in alpine habitats of the Himalayas and central Asia. Commonly referred to as saw-wort or snow lotus, the latter name is specifically used for several high-altitude species in central Asia. These plants are perennial and herbaceous, with their height ranging from small alpine species measuring 5–10 cm to tall, thistle-like plants reaching up to 3 meters. The leaves are arranged in a dense basal rosette and spiral upward along the flowering stem. The flowers are organized into dense heads of small capitula, often surrounded by dense, woolly hairs that range in color from white to purple. The individual florets also exhibit similar coloration. The woolly covering is most pronounced in high-altitude species, serving critical functions such as thermoregulation to minimize frost damage during the night and protection against ultraviolet radiation from intense high-altitude sunlight. The genus was named by De Candolle in honor of Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure (1767–1845). Uses Several high-altitude Himalayan species of Saussurea are cultivated as ornamental plants due to their decorative, dense, woolly flower heads. These plants are among the most challenging to grow, as they are adapted to harsh climates at altitudes of 3500–5000 meters. They require cool temperatures, an extended winter dormancy period lasting up to 8–10 months, and well-drained, humus-rich gravel soils. The dried root of Saussurea lappa, known as costi amari radix or costus root, was a significant item in Roman trade with India. This species is used as an anti-inflammatory agent and is a component of the traditional Tibetan medicine Padma 28. Research has demonstrated that it inhibits the mRNA expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages, thereby reducing nitric oxide production. In laboratory studies on rats, crude ethanolic extracts at doses of 50–200 mg/kg reduced inflammation in standard tests. Additionally, the sesquiterpene fraction of the extract, administered at doses of 25–100 mg/kg, reduced several molecular markers of inflammation. The flowers and stems of Saussurea involucrata have been used in traditional Chinese medicine for treating rheumatoid arthritis, coughs associated with cold, stomachache, dysmenorrhea, and altitude sickness. This species has been found to exhibit anti-inflammatory, cardiotonic, abortifacient, anticancer, and antifatigue properties. Ethanol extracts of this plant have shown analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects at doses of 75–300 mg/kg. However, due to overharvesting, the slow-growing wild plant is endangered. Tissue culture-grown substitutes, which are largely equivalent, have been proposed as an alternative. Despite its medicinal properties, the analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects of Saussurea are generally inferior to those of 10 mg of indomethacin. Notable Species The genus includes numerous species distributed across various regions, such as: Saussurea abnormis (Himalaya) Saussurea americana (American saw-wort, western North America) Saussurea involucrata (Snow lotus, Himalaya, China) Saussurea lappa (Himalaya) Saussurea obvallata (Brahma Kamal, Himalaya, northern Burma, southwest China) Saussurea pygmaea (Alps, Carpathians) Saussurea velutina (China) This list represents only a fraction of the species within the genus, which are distributed across diverse geographic regions, including the Himalayas, China, Russia, and North America.
